dialogues-between-philosophy-religion-et.d: Dialogues between Philosophy & Religion / Ethical Studies & Religion
terms: Evaluation in dialogues
Strong answers weigh whether philosophical and ethical challenges strengthen, modify or undermine religious belief, reaching a justified judgement.
Religion and ethical theory
Dialogues assess how far approaches such as natural moral law, situation ethics or virtue ethics are compatible with the religion's own moral teaching.
Religion and moral authority
Believers locate ethical guidance in sacred texts, leaders, conscience and reason, and dialogues examine how these interact with secular moral philosophy.
Religion and religious experience
Dialogues ask whether the religion treats visions, conversion and mysticism as authoritative revelation or tests such claims against scripture and tradition.
Religion and the problem of evil
A dialogue examines how far evil and suffering challenge the studied religion's idea of God, and how its theodicies and practices respond.
The dialogues approach
This part of the course brings philosophy of religion and ethical studies into conversation with the beliefs and practices of the religion you have studied.

ethics-ethical-theories-natural-law-situ.d: Ethics: Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Virtue Ethics)
terms: Bentham Act 1789
Introduction to the Principles of Morals; greatest happiness for greatest number; hedonic calculus measures pleasures by 7 criteria.
Critiques
Hard to predict consequences; ignores justice (gang rape majority); demands too much; comparing utilities.
Hedonic Calculus
Bentham's 7 factors: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent; calculates utility.
Mill Higher Pleasures
Utilitarianism 1863; qualitative distinction; better Socrates dissatisfied than fool satisfied; rejected pure hedonism.
Preference Utilitarianism
Developed by R.M. Hare and popularised by Peter Singer; maximise satisfaction of preferences, not pleasure; Singer's basis for animal liberation and the drowning child analogy.
Rule Utilitarianism
Mill's refinement: follow rules that maximise utility; avoids problematic act-utility e.g. lying not always wrong.

ethics-issues-of-human-life-death-animal.d: Ethics: Issues of Human Life & Death / Animal Life & Death
terms: Heaven and Hell
Christian eternal communion with God or separation; Islamic Jannah/Jahannam; literal or metaphorical debate.
Immortality of Soul
Plato's Phaedo; soul pre-exists and survives body; influenced Christian thought; tension with biblical resurrection.
Near-Death Experiences
Pim van Lommel, Sam Parnia research; tunnels, lights, life reviews; interpretations vary spiritual vs neurological.
Purgatory
Catholic doctrine of intermediate state of purification; Dante's Purgatorio; rejected by Protestants at Reformation.
Reincarnation
Hindu/Buddhist/Sikh; soul reborn based on karma; aim is liberation (moksha/nibbana); Stevenson investigated cases.
Resurrection
Christianity teaches bodily resurrection (1 Corinthians 15); Islam also affirms; basis is Jesus' rising on third day.

philosophy-of-religion-arguments-for-the.d: Philosophy of Religion: Arguments for the Existence of God
terms: Anselm Ontological
1078 Proslogion: God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; existence in reality greater than mind alone.
Aquinas Five Ways
Summa Theologica 1265-74: motion, cause, contingency, gradation, teleology; demonstrate God a posteriori.
Aristotle Four Causes
Material (what made of), formal (essence), efficient (what brings about), final (purpose); explanation of substances.
Hume's Critique
1779 Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion; teleological argument weak by analogy; world more like vegetable than machine.
Kant Moral Argument
Critique of Practical Reason; God needed as postulate for highest good (virtue + happiness); rejects theoretical proofs.
Plato's Forms
World of unchanging perfect Forms; particulars participate imperfectly; Form of the Good illumines all others (Republic Book 6).
Augustinian theodicy
Augustine saw evil as a privation of good, not a created thing, entering a perfect creation through the free fall of angels and humans.
Free will defence
The argument that genuine human freedom is so valuable that God is justified in permitting the possibility of evil that misused freedom brings.
Logical and evidential problems
Mackie argued God and evil are logically incompatible (the inconsistent triad), while the evidential problem claims the amount of suffering makes God improbable.
Natural and moral evil
Moral evil results from free human choices, such as murder; natural evil arises from the world's workings, such as earthquakes and disease.
Soul-making theodicy
Drawing on Irenaeus, Hick argued the world is a 'vale of soul-making' in which challenge and suffering enable free growth towards God.
The problem of evil
The challenge that the existence of an omnipotent, omnibenevolent God seems incompatible with the reality of evil and suffering in the world.

philosophy-of-religion-religious-experie.d: Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience & Language
terms: Analogy and symbol
Aquinas held that human terms apply to God by analogy rather than literally, while Tillich saw religious language as symbolic participation in ultimate reality.
Challenges to religious experience
Critics offer physiological and psychological explanations, such as drugs, temporal-lobe activity or Freud's wish-fulfilment, and stress verification problems.
Falsification debate
Flew argued believers allow nothing to count against claims like 'God loves us'; Hare's 'bliks' and Mitchell's partisan replied in different ways.
Types of religious experience
Categories include visions, voices, the numinous sense of awe described by Otto, conversion experiences and mystical experiences of union.
Verification principle
Logical positivists such as Ayer held that statements are meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable, dismissing religious claims as meaningless.
William James on mysticism
James identified four marks of mystical experience - ineffability, noetic quality, transiency and passivity - and judged experiences pragmatically by their fruits.

philosophy-of-religion-self-death-afterl.d: Philosophy of Religion: Self, Death & Afterlife
terms: Materialism
The view that persons are wholly physical, so consciousness depends on the brain and death is the end unless the body itself is restored.
Near-death experiences
Reports of out-of-body and tunnel-of-light experiences are cited as evidence of survival, but challenged by physiological explanations such as oxygen deprivation.
Personal identity
Debates about what would make a post-mortem person the same individual: continuity of body, memory or soul, and whether a replica is really you.
Reincarnation and rebirth
Hindu thought teaches reincarnation of the atman according to karma, while Buddhism teaches rebirth without a permanent self (anatta).
Resurrection
The belief that God raises the dead to transformed embodied life; Hick's replica theory defends its logical possibility through divine re-creation.
Substance dualism
Descartes argued mind and body are distinct substances: the mind is a non-physical thinking thing that could in principle survive bodily death.

study-of-religion-christianity-islam-bud.d: Study of Religion: Christianity / Islam / Buddhism / Hinduism / Judaism / Sikhism
terms: Expressions of religious identity
Worship, festivals, pilgrimage, dress and diet - such as the Eucharist, salah or the langar kitchen - express belonging and belief in practice.
Good conduct and key moral principles
Ethical codes such as the Ten Commandments, the Five Precepts or Shari'ah guidance direct believers' behaviour and shape community life.
Religion and contemporary society
Each tradition responds to secularism, science, pluralism and changing views of gender, family and authority in the modern world.
Self, death and the afterlife
Teachings range from resurrection and judgement in Christianity, Islam and Judaism to rebirth shaped by karma in Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism.
Sources of wisdom and authority
Each studied religion grounds belief in sacred texts and authoritative figures - such as the Bible, Qur'an, Torah or Guru Granth Sahib - interpreted within a living tradition.
Ultimate reality
Conceptions of God or the ultimate differ across traditions, from the Trinity in Christianity and Tawhid in Islam to Brahman in Hinduism and nibbana in Buddhism.
Filioque
The Latin clause 'and from the Son', added to the Nicene Creed and disputed by Eastern Christianity.
Homoousios
Greek for 'of the same substance'; the Nicene term affirming the Son's full divinity with the Father.
Hypostasis
Greek term meaning 'person' or 'subsistence', used of the three persons of the Trinity.
Hypostatic Union
The union of divine and human natures in the one person of Christ, defined at Chalcedon (451).
Kenosis
The self-emptying of the Son in the incarnation, drawn from Philippians 2:7.
Perichoresis
The mutual indwelling and interpenetration of the three divine persons.
Analytic Statement
A statement true by virtue of meaning, like 'all bachelors are unmarried'.
Eschatological Verification
John Hick's claim that religious statements will be verified after death, illustrated by the Celestial City parable.
Strong Verification
Requires conclusive empirical proof; Ayer abandoned this as too restrictive.
Synthetic Statement
A statement whose truth depends on the world, established by sense experience.
Verification Principle
A statement is meaningful only if it is analytic or empirically verifiable.
Weak Verification
Requires that some observations be relevant to a statement's probability.
Divine Law
Law revealed through scripture, such as the Decalogue and the Sermon on the Mount.
Eternal Law
God's rational ordering of the universe, fully known only to God himself.
Human Law
Positive law made by states which should reflect Natural Law to be just.
Natural Law
The participation of rational creatures in the Eternal Law, discoverable by reason.
Primary Precepts
Self-preservation, reproduction, education of offspring, living in society, and worship of God.
Synderesis
The innate principle 'do good and avoid evil' which Aquinas calls the first precept.
Anselm's Proslogion
The 1078 work containing the classical ontological argument in two forms.
Aquinas' Five Ways
Five a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologica I, q. 2: motion, causation, contingency, gradation, and governance.
Cosmological
An umbrella term for arguments from the existence, motion, or contingency of the universe to a first cause.
Kalam Argument
Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; therefore the universe has a cause.
Paley's Watchmaker
From Natural Theology (1802): an argument from apparent design to a divine designer.
Teleological
An umbrella term for arguments from apparent design, order, or purpose to a designer.
Anselm's First Form
From Proslogion 2: God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived must exist in reality, not merely in the understanding.
Anselm's Second Form
From Proslogion 3: God cannot be conceived not to exist; necessary existence is a perfection.
Descartes' Version
In Meditation V (1641), God's existence follows from His essence as a supremely perfect being, just as triangles necessarily have three angles.
Kant's Critique
In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Kant argued that 'existence is not a predicate'.
Ontological Argument
An a priori argument that moves from the concept of God to His necessary existence.
Plantinga's Modal Version
If it is possible that a maximally great being exists, then such a being exists in every possible world, including the actual one.
Categorical Imperative
Groundwork of Metaphysics of Morals 1785; act only on maxims that can be universalised; binding regardless of inclination.
Good Will
Only unconditional good; acting from duty not inclination; even successful action not from duty has no moral worth.
Humanity Formula
Second formulation: treat humanity always as end, never merely as means; basis for dignity ethics.
Kingdom of Ends
Third formulation: act as legislator in community of rational beings; ideal moral community of free agents.
Postulates of Practical Reason
Free will, immortality, God; necessary assumptions for moral life though not theoretically demonstrable.
Universalisability
First formulation: act so maxim could become universal law; lying fails since it self-defeats.

an-introduction-to-the-acts-of-the-apost.d: An Introduction to the Acts of the Apostles
terms: Abrahamic religions
Judaism, Christianity, Islam; trace descent from Abraham; monotheistic; share Hebrew Bible/Torah and ethical monotheism.
Comparative method
Friedrich Max Muller's 1870 founding of comparative religion at Royal Institution; 'he who knows one knows none'.
Daoic traditions
Chinese family including Daoism, Confucianism and folk religion; emphasise harmony, yin-yang and ancestor veneration.
Dharmic traditions
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism originating in Indian subcontinent; share karma, dharma and rebirth concepts.
Phenomenology of religion
Ninian Smart's Seven Dimensions of Religion 1989: doctrinal, mythical, ethical, ritual, experiential, social, material.
Religion definition
Emile Durkheim's Elementary Forms 1912: 'unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things'; functionalist sociological approach.

the-early-church-the-church-in-acts.d: The Early Church: The Church in Acts
terms: Conversion of Saul (Acts 9)
An encounter with the risen Christ on the Damascus road transformed Saul from persecutor of the Church into the apostle Paul.
Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
Church leaders agreed that Gentile converts need not be circumcised or keep the whole Jewish Law, opening the Church to the Gentile world.
Life of the first community
Acts 2:42-47 describes believers devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayer, sharing their possessions in common.
Pentecost (Acts 2)
The Holy Spirit descended on the disciples, Peter preached to the crowds, and about three thousand were baptised - the birth of the Church.
Stephen, the first martyr
One of seven chosen to serve the community, Stephen's speech to the Sanhedrin in Acts 7 led to his stoning, witnessed by Saul.
The Gentile mission
Peter's vision and the baptism of Cornelius in Acts 10, followed by Paul's missionary journeys, carried the gospel beyond Judaism.
Markan priority
The widely held scholarly view that Mark was written first and was used as a source by both Matthew and Luke.
Parables and miracles
Jesus taught through comparison stories drawn from daily life, while healings and exorcisms are presented as signs of the kingdom's arrival.
The Kingdom of God
The central theme of Jesus's preaching in the synoptics: God's reign breaking in now and awaited in fullness, taught especially through parables.
The Q source
A hypothetical collection of sayings proposed to explain the material shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark.
The Synoptic Gospels
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share so much material and order that they can be 'seen together', in contrast with the Gospel of John.
The synoptic problem
The puzzle of explaining the literary relationship between the three gospels: who wrote first and who used whom as a source.
Abrahamic religions
Judaism, Christianity, Islam; trace descent from Abraham; monotheistic; share Hebrew Bible/Torah and ethical monotheism.
Comparative method
Friedrich Max Muller's 1870 founding of comparative religion at Royal Institution; 'he who knows one knows none'.
Daoic traditions
Chinese family including Daoism, Confucianism and folk religion; emphasise harmony, yin-yang and ancestor veneration.
Dharmic traditions
Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism originating in Indian subcontinent; share karma, dharma and rebirth concepts.
Phenomenology of religion
Ninian Smart's Seven Dimensions of Religion 1989: doctrinal, mythical, ethical, ritual, experiential, social, material.
Religion definition
Emile Durkheim's Elementary Forms 1912: 'unified system of beliefs and practices relative to sacred things'; functionalist sociological approach.
Actus Purus
'Pure act'; Aquinas' description of God as fully actualised with no potentiality.
Ex Nihilo Nihil Fit
'From nothing, nothing comes'; the principle underlying causal arguments for a first cause.
First Way
Aquinas' argument from motion: whatever is moved is moved by another, and this regress must end in an unmoved mover.
Per Se vs Per Accidens
A distinction between essentially ordered series (which require simultaneous sustaining) and accidentally ordered series (sequential).
Second Way
Aquinas' argument from efficient causation: there must be a first uncaused cause to terminate the regress of causes.
Third Way
Aquinas' argument from contingency: not everything can be contingent, so there must be a necessary being.

christianity-islam-judaism-buddhism-hind.d: Christianity / Islam / Judaism / Buddhism / Hinduism / Sikhism: Social & Historical Developments
terms: Gender and religion
Debates over women's roles in leadership and worship, including arguments about ordination and feminist critiques of traditional teaching.
Reform and renewal movements
Traditions develop historically through reform movements, schisms, revivals and ecumenical efforts that reshape belief and practice.
Religion and science
Traditions respond to scientific accounts such as evolution and cosmology in different ways, ranging from conflict to independence and active dialogue.
Religion, state and society
Each tradition's changing relationship with political power, law and human rights, including questions of religious freedom and influence.
Religious pluralism
Living among many faiths raises questions about truth and salvation, addressed through exclusivist, inclusivist and pluralist positions.
Secularisation
The declining public influence of religion in many Western societies, with ongoing debate over whether religion is disappearing or simply changing.

new-testament-studies-study-of-a-world-r.d: New Testament Studies / Study of a World Religion
terms: Anselm Ontological
1078 Proslogion: God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; existence in reality greater than mind alone.
Aquinas Five Ways
Summa Theologica 1265-74: motion, cause, contingency, gradation, teleology; demonstrate God a posteriori.

philosophy-of-religion-philosophical-iss.d: Philosophy of Religion: Philosophical Issues & Questions
terms: Cosmological argument
Aquinas's first three Ways argue from motion, causation and contingency that the universe depends on an uncaused, necessary being - God.
Design argument
Paley's watch analogy argues that order and purpose in nature, like the parts of a watch, point to an intelligent designer; an a posteriori argument.
Hume's criticisms
Hume attacked the design analogy as weak, noted the universe is unique, and argued the evidence cannot establish one perfect, infinite designer.
Kant's objection
Kant argued that 'existence is not a predicate': adding existence to a concept adds nothing to it, undermining the ontological argument.
Ontological argument
Anselm defined God as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' and argued a priori that such a being must exist in reality.
The Darwinian challenge
Evolution by natural selection explains the appearance of design in living things without invoking a designer, undermining Paley's version.

philosophy-of-religion-problems-of-evil-.d: Philosophy of Religion: Problems of Evil & Suffering
terms: Augustinian type theodicy
Evil is a privation of good entering a perfect creation through the free fall of angels and humans, so God is not evil's author.
Irenaean type theodicy
Hick's soul-making approach: God created immature beings at an 'epistemic distance' so they could freely grow through challenge towards perfection.
Moral and natural evil
Moral evil flows from free human actions such as cruelty; natural evil arises from events like earthquakes, disease and famine.
The evidential problem of evil
The argument that the sheer amount and distribution of suffering, including animal suffering, makes God's existence improbable.
The free will defence
The claim that a world with genuinely free agents is more valuable than one without, even though freedom makes moral evil possible.
The logical problem of evil
Mackie's claim that the set of beliefs - God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, evil exists - is logically inconsistent.

philosophy-of-religion-the-nature-influe.d: Philosophy of Religion: The Nature & Influence of Religious Experience
terms: Challenges to religious experience
Critics cite psychological explanations such as Freud's wish-fulfilment, physiological triggers, and the impossibility of public verification.
Conversion
Experiences that reorient a life, such as Paul on the Damascus road; James distinguished sudden conversions from gradual, volitional ones.
Influence on religious belief
Swinburne's principles of credulity and testimony treat experiences as prima facie evidence for God, while sceptics deny they carry evidential weight.
Rudolf Otto and the numinous
Otto described the heart of religious experience as the numinous: a mystery both awe-inspiring and fascinating, encountered as 'wholly other'.
Types of religious experience
Categories include visions and voices, conversion experiences, mystical union, and corporate experiences shared by groups such as the Toronto Blessing.
William James
James marked mystical experience as ineffable, noetic, transient and passive, and judged experiences pragmatically by their lasting fruits in a person's life.
Application: sexual ethics
Theories are applied to issues such as marriage, cohabitation, contraception and homosexuality, producing sharply different judgements.
Application: war and peace
Just war thinking tests conflicts against criteria such as just cause, legitimate authority and proportionality, while pacifists reject war altogether.
Evaluating ethical theories
Each theory is tested for strengths and weaknesses: utilitarianism's justice problem, situation ethics' unpredictability, and natural law's rigidity.
Natural moral law
Aquinas taught that reason discerns moral precepts from human nature, beginning with primary precepts such as preserving life and living in society.
Situation ethics
Fletcher held that agape love is the only intrinsic good, so rules serve love and may be set aside when love demands it.
Utilitarianism
Bentham's hedonic calculus and Mill's higher pleasures define right action as that which maximises happiness or wellbeing for those affected.

religion-ethics-significant-concepts-in-.d: Religion & Ethics: Significant Concepts in Issues / Debates
terms: Discrimination and justice
Religious and ethical arguments against racism and sexism, alongside critiques that religious institutions have themselves practised discrimination.
Dominion
Interpretations of Genesis 1:28's command to 'rule over' creation; Lynn White blamed this idea for ecological crisis, while defenders read it as responsible rule.
Environmental issues
Debates over climate change, resource use and animal welfare raise questions about human responsibility for the natural world.
Equality
Debates about gender, race and disability draw on ideas such as humans being made in God's image to ground claims of equal dignity and worth.
Secular environmental ethics
Approaches such as conservation ethics, which values nature for human benefit, and deep ecology, which claims nature has intrinsic value.
Stewardship
The view, grounded in Genesis, that humans are caretakers of creation, accountable to God for how the natural world is treated.
Farrer Hypothesis
The view, championed by Austin Farrer and Mark Goodacre, that Luke used Mark and Matthew, dispensing with Q.
Griesbach Hypothesis
The minority view that Matthew was first, Luke used Matthew, and Mark abridged both.
Markan Priority
The dominant scholarly view that Mark was written first and used by Matthew and Luke.
Q Source
A hypothetical sayings document, from German Quelle ('source'), accounting for non-Markan material shared by Matthew and Luke.
Synoptic Gospels
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be 'seen together' due to their parallel material.
Two-Source Hypothesis
The theory that Matthew and Luke independently used Mark and Q.
Contingent Being
A being that exists but might not have existed.
Cosmological Argument
An a posteriori argument from the existence of the cosmos to a transcendent cause.
Fallacy of Composition
Inferring that a whole has a property because its parts do; often raised against cosmological arguments.
Kalam Argument
The Islamic and recently Craigian argument: whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; therefore the universe has a cause.
Necessary Being
A being whose non-existence is impossible; classically identified with God.
Principle of Sufficient Reason
Leibniz's claim that everything has a sufficient reason for its being thus and not otherwise.
Cognitivism
The view that moral statements express beliefs that can be true or false.
Ethical Naturalism
The cognitivist view that moral properties are identical to natural properties.
Intuitionism
Moore's and Ross's view that we know basic moral truths by direct intellectual grasp.
Naturalistic Fallacy
Moore's charge that defining 'good' as any natural property commits a fallacy.
Non-Cognitivism
The view that moral statements express attitudes or commands rather than truth-apt beliefs.
Open Question Argument
Moore's test: for any natural property N, 'is N good?' remains an open question, so good is not identical to N.
Creatio ex Nihilo
The doctrine that God created the universe out of nothing.
Divine Aseity
God's existence from himself; God depends on nothing else.
Divine Simplicity
The classical doctrine that God is not composed of parts.
Imago Dei
The image of God in which Genesis 1:27 says humanity is created.
Providence
God's ordering of all things to their ends.
Theodicy
Leibniz's term for a justification of God's goodness given evil.
Act Utilitarianism
Bentham's view that each individual action should maximise pleasure and minimise pain.
Categorical Imperative
Kant's supreme moral principle: act only on that maxim which you can will to be a universal law.
Good Will
For Kant, the only thing good without qualification; a will that acts from duty, not inclination.
Hedonic Calculus
Bentham's method for measuring pleasure using factors such as intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, and extent.
Hypothetical Imperative
A command of reason that applies conditionally, based on a desired end, contrasted by Kant with the categorical.
Rule Utilitarianism
Mill's refinement: we should follow rules whose general observance maximises happiness.
Divine Law
The law revealed through Scripture, supplementing natural law where reason is insufficient.
Eternal Law
God's rational ordering of all creation; the divine wisdom directing every action and movement.
Human Law
Particular legal codes derived by reason from the natural law to govern communities.
Natural Law
The participation of rational creatures in the eternal law, knowable by reason.
Primary Precepts
The fundamental goods that natural law directs us to: preserve life, reproduce, educate offspring, live in society, and worship God.
Synderesis Rule
The first principle of practical reason: 'good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided'.

developments-in-christian-thought-august.d: Developments in Christian Thought: Augustine, Death & Afterlife, Knowledge of God
terms: Aquinas Summa Theologica
1265-74; synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology; Five Ways; doctrine of analogy for God-talk.
Augustine's Confessions
397-400 AD; spiritual autobiography; original sin; restless heart until rests in God; influenced Western theology.
Bonhoeffer Discipleship
Cost of Discipleship 1937; cheap vs costly grace; resisted Nazis, executed April 1945 at Flossenburg.
Calvin Predestination
Institutes 1536; double predestination of elect and reprobate; sovereignty of God; Geneva theocracy.
Liberation Theology
Gutierrez 1971 A Theology of Liberation; preferential option for poor; Latin American Catholic movement.
Luther Sola Scriptura
1517 95 Theses; salvation by faith alone (sola fide), grace alone, scripture alone; sparked Reformation.

philosophy-of-religion-ancient-philosoph.d: Philosophy of Religion: Ancient Philosophical Influences (Plato, Aristotle)
terms: Aristotle's four causes
Aristotle explained things through material, formal, efficient and final causes, with the final cause - purpose or telos - completing the explanation.
Plato and Aristotle on the soul
Plato saw the soul as immortal and separable from the body, while Aristotle treated the soul as the form of the body, not normally separable.
Plato's Forms
Plato held that beyond the changing world of appearances lie eternal, perfect Forms, which reason alone can know.
The Analogy of the Cave
Plato's image of prisoners mistaking shadows for reality, picturing the philosopher's ascent from illusion to knowledge of the Forms.
The Form of the Good
The highest Form, which Plato likened to the sun: it gives reality to the other Forms and makes knowledge of them possible.
The Prime Mover
Aristotle's eternal, unchanging being that moves the universe as a final cause, attracting motion like an object of desire while thinking only of itself.

philosophy-of-religion-arguments-based-o.d: Philosophy of Religion: Arguments based on Observation & Reason
terms: A posteriori and a priori
Observation-based arguments yield at best probable conclusions, while the reason-based ontological argument claims necessity but rests on definition.
Cosmological argument
Aquinas's first three Ways argue from motion, causation and contingency that there must be a necessary, uncaused being - God.
Gaunilo and Kant's objections
Gaunilo parodied Anselm with a perfect island, and Kant argued that existence is not a predicate that adds to a concept.
Hume's criticisms
Hume attacked the design analogy as weak, suggested alternative explanations, and argued the evidence cannot establish the God of classical theism.
Ontological argument
Anselm argued from reason alone that 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' must exist in reality as well as in the mind.
Teleological argument
Aquinas's fifth Way and Paley's watch argue from order, regularity and purpose in nature to an intelligent designer; arguments from observation.

philosophy-of-religion-religious-experie.d: Philosophy of Religion: Religious Experience, Problem of Evil
terms: Augustinian theodicy
Evil as privation of good entering a perfect creation through the Fall, so that God is not the author of evil.
Challenges to religious experience
Sceptics offer physiological and psychological explanations and argue private experiences cannot be verified as evidence for God.
Hick's soul-making theodicy
An Irenaean approach: God made immature creatures at an epistemic distance, and a challenging world enables free growth towards perfection.
The problem of evil
The challenge that evil and suffering count against an all-powerful, all-loving God: logically (Mackie) or evidentially (from evil's sheer extent).
Types of religious experience
Visions, voices, conversion and mystical experiences, whether individual like Paul's conversion or corporate like the Toronto Blessing.
William James on experience
James marked mystical experiences as ineffable, noetic, transient and passive, and judged them by their practical fruits rather than their causes.

religion-ethics-applied-ethics-euthanasi.d: Religion & Ethics: Applied Ethics (Euthanasia, Business Ethics, Sexual Ethics)
terms: Corporate social responsibility
The debate over whether businesses have duties beyond profit: Friedman's shareholder view against stakeholder theories of wider responsibility.
Euthanasia distinctions
Debates distinguish voluntary from non-voluntary euthanasia and active killing from withdrawing treatment, alongside arguments about assisted dying.
Sanctity and quality of life
The sanctity view holds life is sacred and God-given, while quality-of-life views measure the value of life by wellbeing and autonomy.
Sexual ethics
Premarital and extramarital sex, contraception and homosexuality are assessed through natural law, situation ethics, Kantian and utilitarian approaches.
Theories applied to euthanasia
Natural law appeals to the preservation of life and double effect, while situation ethics asks what agape love requires in each situation.
Whistle-blowing and good ethics
Business ethics asks when exposing wrongdoing is justified and whether good ethics is ultimately good business.
Aquinas on conscience
Conscience is reason at work: synderesis grasps first moral principles and conscientia applies them to actions, so conscience can err through ignorance.
Emotivism
Ayer's non-cognitivist view that moral statements express feelings of approval or disapproval - 'boo/hurrah' - and are neither true nor false.
Freud on conscience
Conscience is the super-ego: internalised parental and social disapproval producing guilt, a psychological rather than divine faculty.
Intuitionism
Moore argued 'good' is a simple, indefinable property known by intuition, and accused naturalists of the naturalistic fallacy.
Meta-ethics
The study of the meaning and status of moral language - what 'good' means and whether moral claims can be true - rather than which acts are right.
Naturalism
The cognitivist view that moral statements describe natural facts about the world, for example identifying goodness with pleasure or flourishing.

religion-ethics-normative-ethical-theori.d: Religion & Ethics: Normative Ethical Theories (Natural Law, Situation Ethics, Kantian, Utilitarianism)
terms: Bentham Act 1789
Introduction to the Principles of Morals; greatest happiness for greatest number; hedonic calculus measures pleasures by 7 criteria.
Critiques
Hard to predict consequences; ignores justice (gang rape majority); demands too much; comparing utilities.
Hedonic Calculus
Bentham's 7 factors: intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity, extent; calculates utility.
Mill Higher Pleasures
Utilitarianism 1863; qualitative distinction; better Socrates dissatisfied than fool satisfied; rejected pure hedonism.
Preference Utilitarianism
Developed by R.M. Hare and popularised by Peter Singer; maximise satisfaction of preferences, not pleasure; Singer's basis for animal liberation and the drowning child analogy.
Rule Utilitarianism
Mill's refinement: follow rules that maximise utility; avoids problematic act-utility e.g. lying not always wrong.
Caritas
Rightly ordered love which refers all created goods to God.
Concupiscence
The disordered desire that remains as a wound even after baptism.
Cupiditas
Disordered love that turns from God to creatures as ends in themselves.
Massa Damnata
The 'lump of damnation' from which God elects some to salvation.
Original Righteousness
The pre-Fall state in which reason rightly governed will and passions.
The Fall
Adam's primal disobedience, transmitted to all his descendants.
Allegory of the Cave
Plato's Republic Book VII image: prisoners mistake shadows for reality until the philosopher escapes to the sun.
Form of the Good
The highest Form in Plato's Republic, which gives intelligibility to other Forms.
Four Causes
Aristotle's material, formal, efficient, and final causes.
Prime Mover
Aristotle's Unmoved Mover in Metaphysics Lambda: a final cause that moves by being the object of love.
Telos
End or purpose; the final cause of a thing.
Theory of Forms
Plato's metaphysics: eternal, immaterial paradigms in which sensible things participate.
Agape
Self-giving love; the only intrinsic good for Fletcher.
Conscience
For Aquinas, the application of moral knowledge to particular acts; for Fletcher, the loving response in situation.
Doctrine of Double Effect
An act with foreseen bad effects may be permissible if the act itself is good, the bad effect is unintended, the good does not flow from the bad, and there is proportionate reason.
Natural Law
The rational participation in eternal law that human beings can discern by reason.
Primary Precepts
Self-preservation, reproduction, education, society, worship of God.
Real and Apparent Good
Aquinas's distinction between what truly perfects human nature and what merely seems.
Bliks
Hare's non-cognitive but action-guiding world-views.
Eschatological Verification
Hick's claim that religious statements are in principle verifiable after death.
Falsification Principle
A genuine assertion must rule out some possible state of affairs.
Strong Verification
Requires conclusive empirical verification.
Verification Principle
A statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
Weak Verification
Requires that some observations be relevant.
A Posteriori
Knowledge or argument derived from sensory experience of the world.
A Priori
Knowledge or argument independent of sensory experience, derived from reason alone.
Cosmological Argument
An a posteriori argument that infers God's existence from the existence and contingency of the universe.
Necessary Being
A being whose non-existence is impossible; in classical theism, God is the only necessary being.
Ontological Argument
An a priori argument from the concept of God as the greatest conceivable being to His necessary existence, originating with Anselm.
Teleological Argument
An a posteriori argument from the apparent design or purpose in nature to a designer, classically presented by William Paley.
Epicurean Paradox
The ancient dilemma: if God is willing but unable, He is impotent; if able but unwilling, malevolent; if both, whence evil?
Evidential Problem
William Rowe's claim that the kinds and quantities of evil we observe make God's existence improbable.
Inconsistent Triad
Mackie's set of three propositions: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists; he argues all three cannot be true together.
Logical Problem
Mackie's claim that the existence of any evil is logically incompatible with an omnipotent and wholly good God.
Moral Evil
Suffering caused by the free choices of moral agents.
Natural Evil
Suffering caused by natural processes such as earthquakes, disease, and animal predation.
Death by a Thousand Qualifications
Flew's charge that theistic statements are progressively qualified until they say nothing.
Falsification Principle
Flew's view that for a statement to be a genuine assertion, the speaker must concede what would count against it.
Strong Verification
A statement is meaningful only if it can be conclusively verified in experience.
University Debate
The 1950-51 'Theology and Falsification' exchange in the Oxford journal University between Antony Flew, R.M. Hare, and Basil Mitchell.
Verification Principle
The logical positivist criterion that a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.
Weak Verification
Ayer's softened version: a statement is meaningful if some observation is relevant to its truth or falsity.
Agape
The Greek New Testament word for unconditional, self-giving love; for Fletcher, the sole moral absolute.
Antinomianism
The rejection of all moral rules and principles, leaving each act unguided.
Legalism
An approach to ethics that rigidly applies prefabricated rules without regard to context.
Pragmatism
Fletcher's first working principle: a proposed course of action must actually work.
Relativism
Fletcher's second working principle: rules are relative to the demand of love in each situation.
Situation Ethics
Joseph Fletcher's 1966 moral theory in which the only intrinsic good is agape love, applied freshly to each situation.
Filioque
The Latin clause 'and from the Son', added to the Nicene Creed in the West to affirm the Spirit's procession from both Father and Son.
Homoousios
'Of one substance'; the term used at Nicaea (325) to affirm that the Son shares the same divine substance as the Father.
Hypostatic Union
The Chalcedonian definition (451) that Christ is one person in two natures, divine and human, 'without confusion or change'.
Incarnation
The doctrine that the eternal Son of God became fully human in Jesus Christ without ceasing to be divine.
Perichoresis
The mutual indwelling or 'dance' of the three persons of the Trinity, expressing their unity in distinction.
Trinity
The Christian doctrine that God is one substance (ousia) in three persons (hypostases): Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
